item.research_question: How can High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) be designed and optimized to simultaneously achieve high saturation magnetization, high electrical resistivity, and high malleability for soft magnetic material applications?
item.material_system: FeCoNi(AlSi)x where x ranges from 0 to 0.8 in molar ratio (alloys denoted A0 to A8)
item.processing_route: Arc-melting pure elements (>99.5 wt.% purity) in high-purity argon atmosphere on a water-cooled Cu hearth, remelted four times for homogeneity; rapid solidification into ingots; compressive testing of cylindrical samples (Φ3 × 6 mm) at room temperature with a strain rate of 2 × 10−4 s−1
item.test_conditions: Room temperature compressive testing; X-ray diffraction (30 kV, 20 mA, Cu target, 10°/min); Electrical resistivity measurement; Magnetization curves via Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS); SEM-EDS microstructural analysis
key_findings: The optimal balance of properties is achieved at x = 0.2 (A2 alloy) with saturation magnetization of 1.15 T, coercivity of 1,400 A/m, electrical resistivity of 69.5 μΩ·cm, yield strength of 342 MPa, and strain without fracture of 50%.
Saturation magnetization (Ms) drops almost monotonically from 1.315 T at x = 0 (A0) to 0.46 T at x = 0.8 (A8) upon Al and Si addition.
Alloys with x ≤ 0.2 exhibit a single-phase FCC solid solution, while x = 0.3 shows a BCC + FCC mixture, and x ≥ 0.4 transitions to almost entirely BCC structure.
Plastic deformation (εp) exceeds 50% without fracture for x in the range of 0 to 0.2, whereas ductility diminishes significantly for x ≥ 0.4, with A8 shattering immediately after elastic deformation.
Electrical resistivity generally increases from x = 0 to x = 0.8, reaching 69.5 μΩ·cm at x = 0.2, which falls within the typical range (50–80 μΩ·cm) of silicon steels.
The A3 alloy (x = 0.3) exhibits a yield strength of 938 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 2,857 MPa with 33% plasticity, attributed to the mixture of FCC and BCC phases.
Coercivity (Hc) is low for x ≤ 0.2 but increases dramatically at x = 0.3 due to phase boundaries hindering domain-wall movement, before falling back at x = 0.5.
item.mechanism: High saturation magnetization in FCC structures is attributed to higher atomic packing density (more ferromagnetic atoms per unit volume) and the absence of anti-parallel magnetic coupling elements like Cr; electrical resistivity increases due to lattice distortion from Al/Si, chemical randomness acting as point defects, and electron scattering; mechanical strength and malleability are governed by the phase composition (FCC favors plasticity, BCC increases lattice resistance) and solid-solution strengthening from lattice distortion.
item.limitations: The text notes that for x ≥ 0.4, ductility diminishes and samples become brittle; the A8 alloy shatters immediately after elastic deformation; coercivity is highly sensitive to microstructure and difficult to predict solely from composition; ab initio calculations systematically overestimate saturation magnetization compared to experiments due to limited system size and ignored impurities/phase segregation.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that coercivity can be tuned within a wide range at a given composition by controlling quenching rates and applying heat/pressure treatments to further reduce Hc; the insights on composition-dependent structures and properties can guide the design of structural and functional HEAs and the development of high-entropy soft magnetic materials.
quotes: the optimal balance of magnetic, electrical, and mechanical properties is achieved at x = 0.2, for which the combination of saturation magnetization (1.15 T), coercivity (1,400 A/m), electrical resistivity (69.5 μΩ·cm), yield strength (342 MPa), and strain without fracture (50%) makes the alloy an excellent SMM.
The FCC-BCC transition with changing composition has been explained from several aspects, such as the valence electron concentration and the lattice distortion and instability.

HEAs with an FCC structure exhibit much higher saturation magnetization than those with a BCC structure. This feature is due to not only their high contents of the ferromagnetic Fe/Co/Ni, but also the higher atomic packing density (or atomic volume fraction) of the FCC structure.
